title: Untitled (working title): the cold open
description: The cold open of an animated 1975 feature: a pilot who sounds amazed, a crate marked INERT, a truck, a near-miss, and a crate that is empty. About six minutes, 8 scenes, 39 shots, almost no dialogue. No pictures yet.

acts.title: Cold open: 1944 to the creek
acts.description: A pilot, a hangar, a truck, a swerve, a fall and an empty crate. Nobody says what it is.

scenes.title: Over Europe, 1944
scenes.description: Black screen. A pilot on the radio, amazed: something is pacing his wing, copying him. A clicking in his headset: three quick, one slow. The order to fire. Gunfire, then silence. We never see what he shot.

scenes.title: Hangar 18
scenes.description: A Senate hearing on a guard-booth TV while airmen empty the hangar. One crate sits apart, stenciled INERT; nobody reads it aloud. The sergeant's coffee ring on its lid, his hand laid flat on it. The trucker signs for AGRICULTURAL EQUIPMENT without looking up.

scenes.title: The back road
scenes.description: Past the weigh station and into the Ohio hills, fog in the hollows, warm dash lights. An unmarked sedan trails. A knock from the trailer, then another; the airman taps his knee along: three quick, one slow. Three knocks. The slow one never comes.

scenes.title: The swerve
scenes.description: A station wagon drifts over the center line; both drivers yank the wheel. The mirror snaps off, a nurse's cap flies out of the window, the trailer fishtails, the missing slow knock lands and the rear doors burst open. Skid or something inside? The crate slides over the edge.

scenes.title: The fall
scenes.description: The crate tumbles down the bank, shedding boards. The camera rides inside: darkness, flashes of light through the cracks, nothing you can make out. It lands by the creek, split open. Silence. Then the crickets.

scenes.title: Topside
scenes.location: EXT. THE ROADSIDE, ABOVE THE BANK
scenes.description: She didn't stop. Road flares in red fog, the sedan screeching up. An agent picks up the white cap and the snapped-off mirror and pockets both. Down the bank.

scenes.title: The crate
scenes.description: Empty. A small hollow in thirty-year-old straw. Every inch of the inside walls scratched with thousands of tiny marks, each with a stroke through it, the newest bright and fresh-cut. It was counting. The far corner, where a few marks are uncrossed, is left in the dark.

scenes.title: Far off in the woods
scenes.location: EXT. THE WOODS ABOVE THE CREEK
scenes.description: Faintly, three quick clicks and one slow, moving away. The agents do not notice; the airman does. The flare sputters out. Black, then the title.

characters.name: Red Two
characters.description: A fighter pilot over Europe, heard and never seen. He sounds amazed, not scared. He does not want to fire.

characters.name: Red Leader
characters.description: Gives the order. Assumes a trick from the Germans ("a Jerry trick").

characters.name: The Airman
characters.description: Sent along in civilian clothes to see the load safely off the base. He is the first to notice the knocks are a rhythm, and the only one who hears the clicks at the end.

characters.name: The Sergeant
characters.description: Has watched these crates for decades. Sets his coffee on the lid out of habit, then rests his hand flat on it, the way you would steady a sleeping animal. Did he know it was awake?

characters.name: The Trucker
characters.description: Thirty years on the road. Signs for AGRICULTURAL EQUIPMENT without looking up. The only joke in the open is his.

characters.name: The Nurse (Mom)
characters.description: Coming off a double shift, window down to stay awake, nodding off at the wheel. Never stops. Never knows what she nearly hit, or what she left behind: her side mirror and her cap.

characters.name: The Agents
characters.description: Arrive in an unmarked sedan. One pockets the nurse's cap and the snapped-off mirror: the thread to the boy's house.

notes.title: Start here: what this is
notes.content: Working title only. This is the cold open of an animated 1970s feature about a boy, a small machine nobody can name, and the people hunting for it. It runs about six minutes: a pilot's voice in 1944, a hangar emptied in 1975, a truck on a back road, a near-miss, a crate that falls, and a crate that is empty. The Screenplay tab holds the pages; the Storyboard has 39 shots with no pictures yet. Acts one to three come next.

notes.title: Seeds the cold open plants
notes.content:
1. The nurse's cap and the snapped-off mirror lead the agents and the detective to the boy's house by different routes.
2. The rhythm (three quick, one slow) ties the airman, the pilot and the machine together before any character notices.
3. The uncrossed marks in the dark corner are the act-two flip: it was not counting days served, it was counting days left. Decide the exact number now; it sets the length of the film's clock.
4. The coffee ring leaves an open question: did the sergeant know it was awake?
5. The airman is the only one who hears the clicks at the end: he is the government's way in to the boy, and the audience's.

notes.title: Rules for the look and the sound
notes.content: Nobody says alien, robot or UFO. Flares, not flashlight beams, outdoors. One recording of the three-quick-one-slow rhythm, used in 1944, in the trailer and in the woods. Never show what the pilot shot; never show what is in the crate. The 1975 setting is deliberate: Church Committee, post-Watergate paranoia, Blue Book already closed.

notes.title: Open questions
notes.content: Title. Why does it move now, after thirty years? How many uncrossed marks (the film's clock)? Is the sergeant the old pilot? Does the airman cross sides? What is the exact count of marks the agents see? The robot's origin stays unexplained: a 1944 shoot-down, bodies and one small machine sent to Wright-Patterson.

brainstorm.title: The boy
brainstorm.content: 11. His mum works double shifts; he is alone at night and rides his bike in the woods. Both of them are waiting for someone who is not coming back. His dad left.

brainstorm.title: The machine
brainstorm.content: Rounded, worn, nothing like a lab. It does not say what it is. It copies sounds. The clicking is its first word.

brainstorm.title: The detective
brainstorm.content: An ex-debunker from Project Blue Book (Wright-Patterson was its headquarters). Spent a career explaining things away; now has to listen to the people he used to dismiss.

brainstorm.title: The battery
brainstorm.content: It has been running on almost nothing for thirty years, playing dead. Being awake with the boy spends what it saved. The marks are the clock.

brainstorm.title: The government
brainstorm.content: Do not know what they have. The scarier for it. They are about to make the same mistake as 1944: shoot first.

script:
Title: Untitled (working title)
Credit: The cold open
Author: [Your Name]
Draft date: October 2026

===

>THE LOOK<

Ohio, 1975, painted rather than photographed: warm dashboard light against blue night, fog in the hollows, wood paneling and station wagons. Soft hand-painted backgrounds and weather; characters drawn plainly and with weight. Small-town Americana that makes something strange feel real.

Nobody in this film ever says "alien", "robot" or "UFO".

>THE SOUND<

Three quick clicks, one slow. It is the same recording over a pilot's headset in 1944, as knocks inside a trailer in 1975, and far off in the woods at the end.

===

INT. COCKPIT, OVER EUROPE - 1944 #1#

BLACK SCREEN. Before any picture, a radio hiss and the drone of an engine.

RED TWO (V.O.)
Red Leader, I've got something on my right wing.

RED LEADER (V.O.)
Say again, Red Two.

RED TWO (V.O.)
No markings. It's glowing. I bank, it banks. It's copying me.

In his headset, a strange clicking, in a distinct rhythm: three quick, one slow.

RED LEADER (V.O.)
Could be a Jerry trick. Take it down.

RED TWO (V.O.)
It's not doing anything. It's just flying with me.

RED LEADER (V.O.)
That's an order.

A long pause. Then gunfire. Then silence. We never see what he shot.

INT. HANGAR 18, WRIGHT-PATTERSON - NIGHT, 1975 #2#

Fade up on Wright-Patterson at night. A TV in the guard booth shows a Senate hearing while airmen quietly empty the hangar.

TV (V.O.)
...the question before this committee is what else has been kept from the American people.

One crate sits apart from the others, stenciled WRIGHT FIELD 1944 - INERT. Nobody reads it aloud.

An old SERGEANT, who has watched these crates for decades, sets his coffee cup on the lid, right into a ring worn into the wood. Then he remembers, and picks it back up. On his way past, he rests his hand flat on the lid, the way you would steady a sleeping animal.

A young AIRMAN hands a clipboard to a civilian TRUCKER.

AIRMAN
Don't you want to know what's in it?

TRUCKER
(signing without looking up)
Nope.

The manifest reads AGRICULTURAL EQUIPMENT.

EXT./INT. TRUCK, BACK ROAD - NIGHT #3#

The truck blows past a sign ordering all trucks into the weigh station. It turns onto a twisting two-lane and climbs into the Ohio hills: fog in the hollows, warm dash lights against the blue night. The Airman rides along in civilian clothes. An unmarked sedan trails a quarter mile back.

TRUCKER
Thirty years driving. First time anybody paid me to skip a scale.

A knock from the trailer. Then another. They both look back.

TRUCKER (CONT'D)
Load's shifting.

The Airman starts tapping his knee along with it, under his breath.

AIRMAN
One-two-three... four. One-two-three... four.

Three quick knocks. The slow one never arrives. He waits, one finger raised, in silence.

TRUCKER
There. Settled.

EXT. THE BEND, BACK ROAD - NIGHT #4#

A station wagon comes around the bend, drifting over the center line. The driver is a NURSE coming off a double shift, window down to stay awake, nodding off. She is the boy's MOM.

MOM
(to herself)
Come on. Two more miles.

Both drivers yank the wheel. The wagon scrapes past; its side mirror snaps off and her nurse's cap flies out of the window. The trailer fishtails, and in the middle of the skid the missing slow knock lands, hard. The rear doors burst open. We cannot tell whether the skid threw them or something inside did.

The crate slides out and over the edge.

EXT. WOODED BANK - NIGHT #5#

The crate tumbles down the wooded bank, slamming into trees and shedding boards. The camera rides inside with it: darkness, flashes of light through the cracks, nothing you can make out.

It lands by the creek, split open. Silence. Then the crickets start up again.

EXT. THE ROADSIDE, ABOVE THE BANK - NIGHT #6#

The wagon's taillights disappear around the bend. She didn't stop.

The Trucker lights road flares. The sedan screeches up and two men in suits get out. One of them, an AGENT, picks up the nurse's cap, white on the black asphalt in the red light, and the snapped-off mirror beside it. He pockets both.

AGENT
Where is it?

TRUCKER
(pointing down the bank, shaking)
Down there. Some lady in a wagon, she just came right at me.

The Agent looks at the white cap in his hand. Then the two agents and the Airman start down the bank through red fog.

EXT. THE CREEK BANK - NIGHT #7#

The crate is empty. A small hollow is pressed into thirty-year-old packing straw, where something lay curled up. A broken board stenciled INERT lies half-sunk in the creek.

An agent holds his flare low to the inside wall, and the light rakes across rows of tiny scratched marks, thousands of them, covering every inch. Each mark has a short stroke cut through it. The newest stroke is bright, fresh-cut wood.

It was counting.

The flare does not reach the far corner, where a few marks are still uncrossed. Nobody looks there.

EXT. THE WOODS ABOVE THE CREEK - NIGHT #8#

Far off in the woods, faintly: three quick clicks and one slow, moving away. The agents don't notice. The Airman does.

AIRMAN
(barely audible, lips moving)
One-two-three... four.

The flare sputters out.

CUT TO BLACK.

TITLE CARD.
